question: A company runs a media streaming platform. Users upload videos that need to be transcoded into multiple formats. Transcoding jobs are CPU-intensive and take 10-60 minutes each. The company needs to process up to 500 jobs simultaneously during peak hours. Which compute approach is MOST cost-effective?

options.text: Always-on EC2 cluster sized for 500 concurrent jobs
AWS Batch with Spot Instances and managed compute environment
Lambda functions (15-minute max doesn't fit 60-minute jobs)
EC2 On-Demand with Auto Scaling

explanation.correct: AWS Batch with Spot Instances: Batch manages job queues and compute environments (EC2/Spot). Jobs are fault-tolerant (transcoding can checkpoint). Spot Instances provide up to 90% cost savings. Batch automatically scales from 0 to 500 instances based on queue depth.

perOption.A: Always-on cluster sized for peak: very expensive when running at 10% capacity most of the time.
perOption.B: CORRECT. AWS Batch: job queue, managed compute environment (EC2 Spot), automatic scale-out for 500 jobs, scale-in when queue empties. Spot for cost savings. Fault-tolerant (Batch retries interrupted Spot jobs).
perOption.C: Lambda max 15 minutes is indeed insufficient for 60-minute jobs. This option is correctly identified as not viable.
perOption.D: On-Demand Auto Scaling works but pays full price. Batch + Spot is more cost-effective for fault-tolerant batch workloads.

question: A company needs EC2 instances in a private subnet to resolve private DNS names for services in the same VPC. They also need to resolve custom on-premises domain names (company.internal) that are hosted on their on-premises DNS server. What enables on-premises DNS resolution from within the VPC?

options.text: Configure the EC2 instances to use the on-premises DNS server IP directly
Create a Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint and forward rules for company.internal
Create a Route 53 private hosted zone for company.internal
Enable DNS hostnames and DNS support in the VPC

explanation.correct: Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint + forwarding rules: EC2 queries → VPC DNS resolver (Route 53 Resolver) → forwarding rule for company.internal → outbound endpoint → on-premises DNS server. VPC DNS for all other names. Clean, scalable solution.

perOption.A: Configuring EC2 instances to use on-premises DNS directly would break VPC DNS resolution for AWS services (they'd query on-premises for everything). Not recommended.
perOption.B: CORRECT. Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint: creates ENIs in VPC subnets for outbound queries. Forwarding rule: company.internal → on-premises DNS IP. All other queries use VPC DNS (Route 53 Resolver default).
perOption.C: Private hosted zone for company.internal in Route 53 would work if you manage the DNS in Route 53. But if the records are on on-premises DNS, creating a hosted zone requires duplicating all records. Forwarding is better.
perOption.D: DNS hostnames and support must be enabled (they are by default in VPCs), but they enable EC2 hostnames and AWS service DNS resolution — not custom on-premises domain forwarding.

question: A company runs 50 EC2 instances for their application. Cost Explorer shows their actual savings from Reserved Instances are lower than expected. AWS Cost Explorer's RI utilization report shows 40% average utilization. What does this mean and how should they fix it?

options.text: Buy more Reserved Instances to cover the unused capacity
The RIs are underutilized — sell unused RI capacity on the RI Marketplace or modify them to match actual usage
The instances are performing below expected CPU levels
40% utilization is normal for Reserved Instances

explanation.correct: 40% RI utilization means they're paying for Reserved Instances capacity that only runs actual workloads 40% of the time. The remaining 60% RI capacity is wasted. Solutions: sell Standard RIs on RI Marketplace, or modify/exchange Convertible RIs for different instance types.

perOption.A: Buying more RIs would make the problem worse — paying for even more underutilized capacity.
perOption.B: CORRECT. Low RI utilization = paying RI rates but not running enough On-Demand instances to benefit. Fix: RI Marketplace (sell Standard RI you don't need), or modify RIs to better-matching instance type, or use Compute Savings Plans (more flexible than RIs).
perOption.C: CPU utilization and RI utilization are different metrics. RI utilization measures whether RI-covered hours are used, not CPU performance.
perOption.D: 40% RI utilization is not normal or acceptable for a pre-paid commitment. Target should be 80%+.

question: A company needs to transfer terabytes of data daily between their on-premises data center and Amazon S3. They have a Direct Connect link. The transfer must be automated, scheduled, and include data integrity verification. Which service is BEST?

options.text: AWS DataSync
AWS Snowball
S3 Transfer Acceleration
rsync over SSH

explanation.correct: AWS DataSync is designed for automated, scheduled data transfers between on-premises and AWS (S3, EFS, FSx). It uses parallel transfers to saturate available bandwidth, includes end-to-end data integrity checksums, and can run over Direct Connect.

perOption.A: CORRECT. DataSync: agent on-premises, transfers to S3 via Direct Connect, scheduling, bandwidth throttling, automatic checksum verification, transfer performance up to 10 Gbps. Perfect for daily automated transfers.
perOption.B: Snowball is for one-time large transfers via physical media shipping. Not for daily automated transfers.
perOption.C: Transfer Acceleration optimizes internet transfers to S3. Not for Direct Connect transfers.
perOption.D: rsync is manual, requires custom scripts, no native AWS integration, no automatic scheduling without cron, no parallel transfer optimization.

question: A company is optimizing costs for their analytics platform. They use Redshift for data warehousing and Athena for ad-hoc queries. S3 stores the raw data. Which TWO changes would MOST effectively reduce analytics costs?

options.text: Convert S3 data from CSV to Parquet format for Athena queries
Use Redshift Spectrum to query S3 data directly instead of loading all data into Redshift
Enable Redshift automatic snapshots every hour
Use S3 Standard storage for all Redshift data
Enable Athena query result caching

explanation.correct: Parquet format reduces Athena scan costs by 30-90%. Redshift Spectrum queries S3 data without ETL loading costs — only compute for the query. Both directly reduce the cost per query/analysis.

perOption.A: CORRECT. CSV to Parquet: columnar format → Athena scans only needed columns. Typical 70-90% reduction in data scanned → 70-90% reduction in Athena query cost. Also compresses better.
perOption.B: CORRECT. Redshift Spectrum: query S3 data in-place without loading into Redshift. Avoid ETL costs, Redshift storage costs for cold data. Pay per TB scanned in S3 (like Athena). Keep only hot data in Redshift.
perOption.C: More frequent snapshots increase storage costs. Doesn't reduce analytics costs.
perOption.D: S3 Standard storage for Redshift data: this doesn't make sense as a standalone option (Redshift uses its own storage). If referring to S3 data lake storage, Standard might be appropriate for frequently accessed data, but not specifically cost-reducing.
perOption.E: Athena query result caching can help for repeated identical queries, but it's not as impactful as columnar format conversion or architecture changes.
